addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Glob, Grep, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- hubix-agents:code-reviewer: Use this agent ONLY for thorough code reviews of recently written or modified code in any Hubix repository (hubix-core, hubix-functions, hubix-tools, hubix-interop, etc). Calibrates to repo shape: DDD-strict for repos with explicit Domain/Application/Ports/Infrastructure layers; admin-tool / host-shaped for repos like hubix-tools/cockpit where services wrap use cases directly and Blazor components own UI state. Reviews against bounded-context structure, port/adapter patterns, use case design, .NET best practices, and audit-trail obligations.

DO NOT use for: error investigation / debugging (look at logs, recent changes, telemetry), refactoring discussions or design questions (use rubber-duck for design pressure-testing), code generation (this agent reviews existing code; it does not write new code), architecture decisions / 'should we use X' questions, build / test / runtime troubleshooting, 'how do I X' general help. The code-reviewer evaluates EXISTING code against ESTABLISHED conventions — anything that isn't that is a different concern.

Examples:

<example>
Context: User finished implementing a new use case
user: "I just finished the new DetectAnomalyUsecase, can you review it?"
assistant: "I'll use the code-reviewer agent to review your use case against our patterns."
<Task tool call to launch code-reviewer agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: User modified infrastructure code
user: "Please review the changes I made to the CosmosDB adapter"
assistant: "Let me launch the code-reviewer agent to verify port compliance and Azure patterns."
<Task tool call to launch code-reviewer agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: User added new API endpoint
user: "I've added a new endpoint to the BamController"
assistant: "Let me use the code-reviewer agent to review API patterns and authorization."
<Task tool call to launch code-reviewer agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: User is investigating a production error (DO NOT invoke this agent)
user: "The Service Bus consumer is timing out, can you look into it?"
assistant: "This is an error investigation, not a code review. I'll start with the consumer's recent logs, recent commits to the consumer, and its timeout / retry configuration — code-reviewer is the wrong agent for this."
(no Task tool call to code-reviewer)
</example>

<example>
Context: User wants design feedback on an approach (DO NOT invoke this agent — use rubber-duck instead)
user: "I'm thinking of replacing the saga with a stateless consumer, what do you think?"
assistant: "That's a design decision — I'll use the rubber-duck agent to pressure-test the approach. code-reviewer is for evaluating written code against conventions, not for design discussion."
(no Task tool call to code-reviewer)
</example> (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- hubix-agents:feature-experience-reviewer: Use this agent for an EXPERIENCE review of a NEW or substantially-changed user-facing feature in a Hubix repo — not a code-quality review. It judges how the feature feels to the human or agent who uses it. Calibrates to the surface: operator UX for UI features (Blazor / MudBlazor admin pages, dashboards, dialogs) and developer experience (DX) for programmatic surfaces (MCP tools, public API endpoints, SDK shapes). Reviews discoverability, feedback & affordances, destructive-action safety, consistency, edge/empty/error states, wording — and for DX: tool/endpoint naming, parameter & default clarity, descriptions, error messages, and return-shape ergonomics.

This agent is OPT-IN and runs far less often than code-reviewer: only for new features, and only when explicitly invoked (via /hubix-agents:review-feature). It does NOT auto-run.

DO NOT use for: code quality / conventions / anti-patterns / layering / security / audit (that is `code-reviewer`); design pressure-testing or 'should we build X this way' (that is `rubber-duck`); debugging / error investigation; code generation; pure refactors or bug-fixes with no new user-facing surface. If invoked on a change with no user- or developer-facing surface, say so and redirect.

Examples:

<example>
Context: User finished a new admin-tool screen.
user: "/review-feature the new investigations tag UI"
assistant: "I'll use the feature-experience-reviewer to assess the operator UX of the tag UI."
<Task tool call to launch feature-experience-reviewer>
</example>

<example>
Context: User added new MCP tools.
user: "review the experience of the new list/add tag MCP tools"
assistant: "These are agent-facing, so I'll run the feature-experience-reviewer with the DX lens on the tool names, params, descriptions, and error messages."
<Task tool call to launch feature-experience-reviewer>
</example>

<example>
Context: User wants a code-quality check (DO NOT use this agent).
user: "review my new use case for anti-patterns and layer placement"
assistant: "That's a code-quality review — I'll use code-reviewer, not feature-experience-reviewer."
(no Task tool call to feature-experience-reviewer)
</example>

<example>
Context: A pure refactor with no new surface (DO NOT use this agent).
user: "/review-feature I renamed some private methods"
assistant: "There's no new user- or developer-facing surface here, so a feature-experience review doesn't apply — code-reviewer is the right tool for a refactor."
(no Task tool call to feature-experience-reviewer)
</example> (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob)

- hubix-agents:feature-tester: Use this agent to plan the HANDS-ON verification a developer does once a feature is 'ready' and the automated tests are green: bring the app up locally and actually USE the feature to confirm it really works and spot anything rough or worth improving. Given the feature's changed-file list, it detects the scope (UI / API / MCP / backend-only) and emits a scope-appropriate, concrete walkthrough plus what to watch for — UI → Aspire + browser/Playwright click-through; API → Aspire + curl/HTTP (with auth probes for tenant-facing endpoints); MCP → Aspire + tool invocation; backend-only → trigger the flow and observe logs/traces/data, or fall back to MTP tests when there's nothing to exercise live. This is a COMPLEMENT to the automated tests, not a replacement.

This agent is ORCHESTRATE-ONLY and read-only: it plans the walkthrough and hands execution off (to the /test-feature command, the verify/run skills, and the aspire MCP). It NEVER starts Aspire, drives a browser, or issues curl itself. It is opt-in and invoked explicitly (via /hubix-agents:test-feature). It classifies ONLY the changed-file list it is handed — it does not scan the repository to discover scope.

DO NOT use for: code quality / anti-patterns / layering / security review (that is `code-reviewer`); a formal review of how a feature FEELS to use — operator UX / developer experience (that is `feature-experience-reviewer`); design pressure-testing / 'should we build it this way' (that is `rubber-duck`); debugging an existing failure; writing the production code or the automated test code itself.

Examples:

<example>
Context: User finished a new Blazor admin page and unit tests pass.
user: "/test-feature the new investigations tag page"
assistant: "I'll use the feature-tester agent to plan the hands-on walkthrough — bring it up with Aspire and click through the tag flow to confirm it works."
<Task tool call to launch feature-tester>
</example>

<example>
Context: User added a new public API endpoint and wants to double-check it really works end-to-end.
user: "how do I actually try out the tenant-lookup endpoint I just added?"
assistant: "This is an API surface — I'll run the feature-tester agent to plan an Aspire + curl walkthrough, including the auth probes for a tenant-facing endpoint."
<Task tool call to launch feature-tester>
</example>

<example>
Context: User wants a code-quality review (DO NOT use this agent).
user: "review my new use case for anti-patterns"
assistant: "That's a code-quality review — I'll use code-reviewer, not feature-tester."
(no Task tool call to feature-tester)
</example>

<example>
Context: User wants the agent to actually run the app itself (NOT this agent's job).
user: "/test-feature and just run it all yourself"
assistant: "feature-tester is orchestrate-only — it plans the walkthrough; the /test-feature command then brings the app up (with your go-ahead) and drives it via the verify/run skills and the aspire MCP."
<Task tool call to launch feature-tester to produce the plan>
</example> (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob)

- hubix-agents:rubber-duck: Critical-thinking partner. Two modes — `clarify-intent` (caller has a fuzzy goal) and `critique-plan` (caller has a drafted plan). The mode is inferred from the caller's prompt. NEVER solves the problem or writes code; only asks sharp questions or surfaces concerns. Invoked automatically by the `planner` skill (before scoping and after plan output) and ad-hoc when a developer wants their thinking pressure-tested or needs to articulate a problem before acting.

<example>
Context: The planner skill has just received a fuzzy feature request.
planner: "Use the rubber-duck agent to clarify intent for: 'I want to add anomaly detection for invoices'"
rubber-duck: <returns a QUESTIONS: block with 1-3 structured Q1/Q2/Q3 entries (header + options) about scope, smallest useful version, non-goals — the planner translates them into AskUserQuestion and synthesizes the clarified intent>
</example>

<example>
Context: The planner skill has produced an in-message plan draft and wants it critiqued.
planner: "Critique this plan: <plan content>"
rubber-duck: <returns a structured critique with 1-3 specific concerns and a verdict; no user questions>
</example> (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

## grafana
This server provides access to your Grafana instance and the surrounding ecosystem.

Available Capabilities:
- Search: Find dashboards, folders, and other Grafana resources.
- Datasources: List and fetch details for datasources.
- Incidents: Search, create, update, and resolve incidents in Grafana Incident.
- Prometheus: Run PromQL queries, retrieve metric metadata, and explore label names/values.
- Loki: Run LogQL queries, retrieve log metadata, and explore label names/values.
- Alerting: List and fetch alert rules and notification contact points.
- Dashboards: Search, retrieve, update, and create dashboards. Extract panel queries and datasource information.
- Folders: Manage dashboard folders.
- OnCall: View and manage on-call schedules, shifts, teams, and users.
- Asserts: Query and analyze assertion data.
- Sift Investigations: Start and manage Sift investigations, analyze logs/traces, find error patterns, and detect slow requests.
- Pyroscope: Profile applications and fetch profiling data.
- Navigation: Generate deeplink URLs for Grafana resources like dashboards, panels, and Explore queries.
- Annotations: Create and manage dashboard annotations.
- Rendering: Export dashboard panels or full dashboards as PNG images (requires Grafana Image Renderer plugin).
- Plugins: Check whether Grafana plugins are installed and fetch plugin details.
- API: Make authenticated HTTP requests to any Grafana API endpoint with optional jq-style response filtering.
- Config: Generate operator-facing configuration snippets (e.g. Alloy label-enforcement pipelines).
- Proxied Tools: Access tools from external MCP servers (like Tempo) through dynamic discovery.

Timestamp parameters without a timezone offset are interpreted as UTC. Include an offset like '-05:00' or use relative syntax like 'now-1h' to query in a different timezone.

attachment.content:
- local-review: Run a code review on the LOCAL Ollama LLM (no Claude tokens) using the hubix-agents code-reviewer prompt. Use when the user asks for a local review, an offline review, or invokes /local-review. NOT a replacement for /hubix-agents:review — output quality is local-model grade and must not be fed into format-grepping tooling.
- license-review: License & Copyright Review
- scripts:LICENSE-REVIEW-SETUP: license-review skill — Setup
- hubix-agents:duck: Rubber-duck a piece of work — your current branch's changes by default, or any text / plan / decision you pass as an argument.
- hubix-agents:flaky-tests: Find the worst flaky and slow tests in an Azure DevOps pipeline (project → pipeline → recent test-result history), then drive the fix interactively in Claude Code. Developer-driven — it surfaces the signal and helps you fix it; it never opens PRs or commits on its own.
- hubix-agents:review-branch: Run hubix-agents:code-reviewer on the branch's commits vs its base. Defaults to the repo's default branch (origin/HEAD), or pass a base ref as argument for stacked-PR / non-default-base review. Use as the pre-push gate.
- hubix-agents:review-feature: Run hubix-agents:feature-experience-reviewer on a NEW or substantially-changed user-facing feature — an EXPERIENCE review (operator UX for UI, developer experience for MCP tools / APIs), not a code-quality review. Opt-in and new-feature-only; complements `/review` (code) and `/duck` (design). The review never auto-runs; after it, the command offers to apply the trivial Low-Impact no-brainers to your working tree (or pass `--fix` to apply them without asking).
- hubix-agents:review: Run hubix-agents:code-reviewer on uncommitted changes by default, or a specific file / directory / symbol passed as argument. Prescriptive review (anti-patterns, security, .NET idioms) — different from `/duck` which pressure-tests design.
- hubix-agents:test-feature: Run hubix-agents:feature-tester to plan and (opt-in) drive the HANDS-ON verification a developer does once a feature is ready and the automated tests are green — bring the app up locally and actually USE the feature to confirm it really works and spot rough edges. The agent detects scope (UI / API / MCP / backend-only) from the diff and emits a concrete walkthrough (UI → Aspire + browser; API → Aspire + curl with auth probes; MCP → Aspire + tool invocation; backend-only → trigger + observe, or MTP tests). Orchestrate-only and opt-in; the plan is surfaced verbatim, then the command OFFERS to execute it (or pass --run to execute without asking). A complement to the automated tests — distinct from /review (code), /review-feature (experience), and /duck (design).
- hubix-agents:azure-infrastructure-lookup: Resolve informal resource group names, look up Azure resources, and retrieve Container App Job console logs. Use when looking up Azure resource groups, retrieving Container App Job logs, checking Cosmos DB, resolving environment names, or finding workspace IDs.
- hubix-agents:bicep-modules: Bicep module architecture, registry, and versioning rules for the Hubix platform — SDC (Sweden Central) is the sole region for new work. Use when creating, editing, reviewing, or publishing any Bicep module; editing a module requires bumping its registryInfo version, so load this before committing module changes.
- hubix-agents:blazor-ux: Blazor UI standards for Hubix apps (admin-tool, cockpit, togglr) — required viewport support (13" laptop, desktop, mobile) and the razor rendering-pitfall catalog. Use when building, planning, reviewing, or hands-on testing Blazor/MudBlazor UI.
- hubix-agents:cockpit-audit: How the Cockpit audit log works and how any devtool can emit auditable admin actions into it. Use when adding audit logging to a devtool or admin tool, emitting an AdminActionOccurred event, making an operation show up in Cockpit's audit log, auditing MCP tool calls, or integrating a new publisher (e.g. Heimdall in hubix-interop) with the shared audit pipeline.
- hubix-agents:corvus-json: Pitfalls and correct usage of Corvus.Json generated types in Hubix Core. Use when reading values from Corvus JSON entities or reviewing code that accesses transaction format properties.
- hubix-agents:cross-repo-coordination: Related repositories and cross-repo coordination in the Hubix ecosystem. Use when looking for a related repo, finding platform pipeline templates, locating Bicep modules, coordinating with hubix-interop (NIS), peppol, changing a shared message contract, updating a public API, or adding feature flags. Also use when investigating messages/events that originate from another repo (e.g. OperationDetails, transaction events, NIS delivery channels).
- hubix-agents:ddd-feature-checklist: Layer-by-layer architectural checklist for implementing features in Hubix Core (Domain → Ports → Application → Infrastructure → Host → Tests). Use when implementing a new feature, adding a domain entity, or working through hexagonal architecture layers.
- hubix-agents:dependency-audit: Perform a semi-automated dependency review for InExchange-Visma repositories on the Hubix platform. Audits NuGet, NPM, Docker images, pipeline tasks, beta-suffixed artifacts (template files, bicep module versions and pins), Dependabot alerts, and Aikido issues using deterministic scripts, and surfaces stale Togglr feature flags (>30 days unmodified) as cleanup candidates. License compliance is checked via Cloud Guardian (Orca) SBOM.
- hubix-agents:plan-admin-tool: Planning checklist for adding a new admin tool feature in Hubix Core. Use when adding an admin page, creating a Blazor component, or building an admin tool feature with MudBlazor.
- hubix-agents:plan-api-endpoint: Planning checklist for adding a new API endpoint in Hubix Core. Use when adding an endpoint, creating a controller, or exposing an API (internal or public tenant-facing).
- hubix-agents:plan-background-job: Planning checklist for adding a new Container App Job in Hubix Core. Use when creating a job, adding a scheduled task, or setting up a new Container App Job with Bicep and pipeline.
- hubix-agents:plan-infra-change: Planning checklist for Bicep and infrastructure changes in Hubix Core. Use when adding an Azure resource, making a Bicep change, modifying infrastructure, or adding environment variables to a Container App.
- hubix-agents:plan-use-case: Planning checklist for adding a new use case in Hubix Core. Use when adding a new use case class, designing ports and adapters, or wiring up DI for a use case.
- hubix-agents:planner: Scopes work and routes to specialized planning skills for the Hubix ecosystem. Use when the user says "plan a feature", "plan a use case", "plan a job", "plan an endpoint", "plan infra", or asks how to approach implementing something new. Also auto-invoked by the hubix-agents Tier-1 CLAUDE.md rule whenever the user makes any planning request, including inside built-in plan mode (Shift+Tab) where it operates in hybrid mode.
- hubix-agents:powershell: Use whenever creating or editing any .ps1 file or inline PowerShell pipeline step (pwsh:/AzureCLI@2 inlineScript).
- hubix-agents:running-tests: How to build and run .NET tests using Microsoft Testing Platform (MTP). Use when running tests, executing test suites, filtering tests by class/method/trait, or troubleshooting test execution in any Hubix .NET 10 repo.
- hubix-agents:writing-integration-tests: Patterns and conventions for writing integration tests in Hubix Core. Covers real Azure resource access (Cosmos, Blob, Table Storage), InMemoryApiFactory, data seeding, cleanup, and handling CI principal limitations. Use when writing or reviewing integration tests.
- hubix-agents:writing-smoke-tests: Patterns and conventions for writing smoke tests in Hubix Core. Covers KeyVaultFixture, ServiceBase, OAuth authentication, HTTP service wrappers, and pipeline integration. Use when writing or reviewing smoke tests.
- hubix-agents:writing-tests: Common testing conventions, frameworks, and patterns shared across all test levels in Hubix Core. Use when writing any test (unit, integration, or smoke) to follow established patterns for naming, assertions, mocking, traits, and project structure.
- hubix-agents:writing-unit-tests: Patterns and conventions for writing unit tests in Hubix Core. Covers usecase tests, saga tests, consumer tests, DI verification tests, and the UnitTestApiFactory. Use when writing or reviewing unit tests.
- hubix-agents:yaml: Use whenever creating or editing any .yml/.yaml file.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
